label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Assume every nontrivial zero of $\zeta$ has real part at most $7/8$.
Then
\[
 \Lambda\le\frac{13963}{100000}=0.13963.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:head
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Initially all zeros in this finite region are real. The classical strip
bound gives $|\operatorname{Im} z|\le1$ throughout the time interval. If the
conclusion fails, consider the closed set of zero-time pairs with
$0\le x\le X$, $1/5\le y\le1$, and $0\le t\le1/5$.
It is compact and disjoint from $t=0$, so its least time $t_1>0$
is attained. No zero can enter across $x=X$ at height at least $1/5$,
by \eqref{eq:wall}; the same holds at $x=-X$ by symmetry.
Continuity of zeros therefore forces a first contact at height
$h=1/5$. We do not need continuity of the unrestricted maximum over
a window whose vertical sides other zeros can cross.
At a first contact in $0\le x\le X$, the right
boundary is excluded by \eqref{eq:wall}. The imaginary axis is zero-free
because $H_t(iy)$ is an integral of a positive integrand.
A multiple contact is excluded by backward Hermite splitting as in
\cite[Proposition 3.1(ii)]{P}: a zero of multiplicity $m\ge2$ at
$z_1=x_1+ih$ has, at time $t_1-v$, a neighbouring zero
$z_1+i\sqrt{2v}\lambda_m+O(v)$, where $\lambda_m>0$ is the largest
root of the probabilists' Hermite polynomial. Its imaginary part is
larger than $h$ for small $v>0$, contradicting first contact. Because
the contact is away from the vertical sides, this earlier zero remains
inside the finite region.

For a simple contact zero $x+ih$, its own conjugate contributes $-1/h$
to its vertical velocity. Every other conjugate pair contributes $-2K_h$,
where
\[
 K_h(d,v)=\frac{h-v}{d^2+(h-v)^2}
          +\frac{h+v}{d^2+(h+v)^2}
 =\frac{2h(d^2+h^2-v^2)}
        {[d^2+(h-v)^2][d^2+(h+v)^2]}.
\]
Pairs with $v\le h$ have nonnegative contribution to $K_h$.
A pair with $v>h$ lies outside $[-X-1,X+1]$ by first contact and
\eqref{eq:wall}, so $|d|\ge1$ and $v\le1$ imply $K_h>0$.
Real zeros carry half-pair weight. Thus $h'\le-1/h<0$, contradicting
first contact from below. Compactness of the finite rectangle and
continuity of zeros justify attainment of a first contact.

label: lem:approx
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the exact heat-convolution decomposition in
\cite[equations (39)--(41)]{P} and its Proposition 6.2 for the
Riemann--Siegel coefficients at arbitrary real part. For the summands
we recover the bound of its Proposition 6.1 using a vertical Stirling
estimate. We do not apply its Theorem 1.3 or Proposition 6.3 at these
larger heights.

\emph{Source formulas and their domains.}
Here we restate the inputs with their original equation numbers.
For $g^*(s)=\overline{g(\overline s)}$, equation (39) of~\cite{P} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:decomposition}
 H_t(z)=\sum_{n\le N}r_{t,n}(v)+\sum_{n\le N}r_{t,n}^*(w)
             +R_{t,N}(v)+R_{t,N}^*(w).
\end{equation}
It holds for $t>0$, $\operatorname{Re} z\ne0$, and every integer $N\ge0$.
Writing
\[
 \mathcal M(s)=\frac{s(s-1)}{16}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2),\qquad
 I_N(s)=\int_{N\swarrow N+1}
       \frac{u^{-s}e^{i\pi u^2}}{e^{\pi iu}-e^{-\pi iu}}\,du,
\]
equations (37)--(38) give $r_{0,n}(s)=\mathcal M(s)n^{-s}$ and
$R_{0,N}(s)=\mathcal M(s)I_N(s)$. The contour is directed southwest
across $(N,N+1)$. Equations (40)--(41) say that, for either of these
functions $g_0$ and its Gaussian evolution $g_t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shifted-heat}
 g_t(s)=e^{-t\eta^2/4}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\sqrt t V\eta}
  g_0(s+\sqrt t V+t\eta/2)\frac{e^{-V^2}}{\sqrt\pi}\,dV,
\end{equation}
provided $\operatorname{Im} s$ and $\operatorname{Im}(s+t\eta/2)$ have the same nonzero sign.

For real $u$, $T'>0$, $a=\sqrt{T'/(2\pi)}$, $N=\lfloor a\rfloor$,
and $\rho=1-2(a-N)$, Proposition 6.2 gives, for every integer $K\ge1$,
\begin{gather}
 I_N(u+iT')=\omega_N a^{-u}
     \left(\sum_{k=0}^K\frac{C_k(\rho,u)}{a^k}
                           +RS_K(u+iT')\right),\label{eq:RS-source}\\
 \omega_N=(-1)^{N-1}
   \exp\left[-i\left(\frac{T'}2\log\frac{T'}{2\pi}
                         -\frac{T'}2-\frac\pi8\right)\right].\notag
\end{gather}
Its equations (53) and (58) give
\[
 C_0(\rho,u)=C_0(\rho)=
 \frac{e^{\pi i(\rho^2/2+3/8)}-i\sqrt2\cos(\pi\rho/2)}
      {2\cos(\pi\rho)},\qquad |C_0(\rho)|\le\tfrac12,
\]
with removable values at $\rho=\pm1/2$. Its equations (54)--(57) are
\begin{align}
 |C_k(\rho,u)|&\le\frac{\sqrt2}{2\pi}
            \frac{9^u\Gamma(k/2)}{2^k} &&(u>0,\ k\ge1),\label{eq:C-positive}\\
 |C_k(\rho,u)|&\le P_0\,2^{-u}\Gamma(k/2)\kappa_0^k
                  &&(u\le0,\ k\ge1),\label{eq:C-negative}\\
 |RS_K(u+iT')|&\le\tfrac17\,2^{3u/2}\Gamma((K+1)/2)(1.1/a)^{K+1}
                  &&(u\ge0),\label{eq:RS-positive}\\
 |RS_K(u+iT')|&\le\tfrac12(9/10)^{\lceil-u\rceil}
               \Gamma((K+1)/2)(1.1/a)^{K+1}
                  &&(u<0,\ K+u\ge2),\label{eq:RS-negative}
\end{align}
where $P_0=\sqrt2/(4\pi^2)$ and
$\kappa_0=((3-2\log2)\pi)^{-1/2}$. There is no upper bound on $K$
and no lower bound on $u$; the negative-part remainder requires
exactly the displayed condition $K+u\ge2$.

\emph{A uniform vertical Stirling estimate.}
Euler--Maclaurin gives, on the slit plane,
\begin{align*}
 \theta(z)&=\log\Gamma(z)-(z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log} z+z-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)\\
 &=\frac1{12z}-\frac1{360z^3}
   -\frac14\int_0^\infty\frac{B_4(\{u\})}{(z+u)^4}\,du.
\end{align*}
Here the branch of $\log\Gamma$ is continued from the positive real
axis. The integral is holomorphic off the nonpositive real axis, so
analytic continuation extends the identity from $\operatorname{Re} z>0$.
Since $|B_4|\le1/30$ and
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(u^2+v_0^2)^{-2}\,du=\pi/(2v_0^3)$,
for $v_0=|\operatorname{Im} z|>1$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vertical-stirling}
 |\theta(z)|\le\frac1{12v_0}
       +\frac{1/360+\pi/240}{v_0^3}
       <\frac1{12(v_0-1)}.
\end{equation}
This estimate is uniform in the real part, including its unbounded
negative tail.

\emph{Elementary normalizer bounds.}
For $s=\sigma+ix/2$, $-3\le\sigma\le4$, direct differentiation gives
\begin{gather*}
 |\alpha(s)-L/2-i\pi/4|\le\frac8{x-20},\qquad
 |\alpha'(s)|\le\frac1{x-6},\\
 \operatorname{Re}\alpha(w)\ge L/2,\qquad
 |\gamma|\le e^{10^{-8}y}\mathcal Q^{-y/2},\qquad
 s_A=\overline{s_B}-y+\kappa,\quad
 |\kappa|\le\frac{ty}{2(x-6)}.
\end{gather*}
The first derivative bound also holds for arbitrary real $\sigma$.
For example, integrate the real part of
$\alpha+(t/2)\alpha\alpha'$ between the two real parts to obtain the
bound for $\gamma$. All errors needed here are bounded by multiples of
$(L+1)/(x-20)$; that quotient is decreasing in this range. Also
$N\ge60000$, $\log N\le L$, and $N^{|\kappa|}<1.000001$.

\emph{Errors in the summands.}
To check the contour estimates explicitly, put $s=\sigma+iT$,
$T=x/2$, $\alpha_n=\alpha(s)-\log n$, and
$\Delta=\sqrt t V+t\alpha_n/2$ in \cite[equation (40)]{P}.
The shifted contour has imaginary part at least $T-0.08$.
Taylor's formula and \eqref{eq:vertical-stirling} bound the absolute
value of the error in the complex exponent by
\[
 \frac{tV^2/2+t^2|\alpha_n|^2/8+1/6}{T-3.08}.
\]
Indeed, $|\Delta|^2\le2tV^2+t^2|\alpha_n|^2/2$ and
$|\alpha'|\le[2(T-3.08)]^{-1}$ along the Taylor segment.
Integration against $e^{-V^2}/\sqrt\pi$ then bounds the relative
error by
\[
 \exp\left(\frac{t^2|\alpha_n|^2/8+t/4+1/6}{T-3.33}\right)-1,
\]
because $(1-t/[2(T-3.08)])^{-1/2}
\le \exp(t/[4(T-3.33)])$. This is the bound in
\cite[Proposition 6.1]{P}, now obtained with a Stirling estimate
uniform on the entire shifted contour. In our domain it is at most
$e^{d(x)}-1$, where we may take
\[
 d(x)=\frac{L^2/400+0.626}{x-6.66}<10^{-10}.
\]
Indeed, for $n\le N$,
$|\alpha-\log n|^2\le\frac14\log^2(\mathcal Q/n^2)+0.667$.
The function $d$ decreases, and $L<23$ at $x=6\cdot10^{10}$.
Combining the heat weights before estimating gives
\[
 |e^{t\log^2n/4}n^{-s_B}|\le n^{-(1+y)/2}\le n^{-2}.
\]
The reflected-to-first magnitude ratio is at most $1.01$, using
$n\le N$ and $N^2\le\mathcal Q+1/80$. Thus the sum of the absolute
main-term weights of both sums is below $4$, since
$2.01\zeta(2)<4$, and their total error
is below $10^{-8}$.

\emph{Errors in the two remainder integrals.}
Here are details of the real-part extension. They also control the
unbounded negative tail in the Gaussian integral.
Write $T=x/2$, $T'=T+\pi t/8$, $a=\sqrt{T'/(2\pi)}$, and $A=T-3$.
For $-3\le\sigma\le4$, the remainder has the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:R}
 R_{t,N}(\sigma+iT)=\omega_Ne^{i\pi\sigma/4}
 e^{t\pi^2/64}M_0(iT')\{C_0+\varepsilon_\sigma\},
 \qquad |\omega_N|=1,
\end{equation}
where $|C_0|\le1/2$. We claim the deliberately loose bound
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eps}
 |\varepsilon_\sigma|\le
 \frac{0.3\,9^\sigma+0.04\,2^{-\sigma}}{a-1}+10^{-8}<\frac1{25}.
\end{equation}

On the shifted contour in \eqref{eq:shifted-heat}, put
$U=\sigma+\sqrt t V$, where $V$ has density $e^{-V^2}/\sqrt\pi$.
Choose the shift $\beta_N=i\pi/4$. The Stirling estimate
\eqref{eq:vertical-stirling} and Taylor expansion of $\log M_0$
about $iT'$ bound the error $E(U)$ in the complex exponent by
\[
 \frac{U^2+6|U|+2/3}{4A}\le\frac{U^2+1}{A}.
\]
Indeed $\alpha(iT')=\log a+i\pi/4+e_0$ with
$|e_0|\le3/(2T')$, and $|\alpha'|\le1/(2A)$ on the horizontal
segment. Inserting \eqref{eq:RS-source} into
\eqref{eq:shifted-heat} cancels $a^{-U}$ and the phase depending
on $V$, and gives exactly
\[
 \frac{R_{t,N}(\sigma+iT)}
      {\omega_N e^{i\pi\sigma/4}e^{t\pi^2/64}M_0(iT')}
 =\mathbb E\left[e^{E(U)}
       \left(C_0+\sum_{k=1}^{K(U)}\frac{C_k(\rho,U)}{a^k}
                    +RS_{K(U)}(U+iT')\right)\right].
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:R} is derived here, and is not an application of
Polymath's Proposition 6.3 outside its stated domain.
With $D=1-t/A$, Gaussian completion yields
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E e^{(U^2+1)/A}-1
 &\le D^{-1/2}e^{17/A+16t/(A^2D)}-1<10^{-8},\\
 0.2\,\mathbb E(9^Ue^{(U^2+1)/A})
 &\le0.2\,9^\sigma D^{-1/2}
       e^{17/A+t(\log3+4/A)^2/D}<0.3\,9^\sigma,\\
 0.029\,\mathbb E(2^{-U}e^{(U^2+1)/A})
 &\le0.029\,2^{-\sigma}D^{-1/2}
       e^{17/A+t(\log2/2+4/A)^2/D}<0.04\,2^{-\sigma}.
\end{align*}
These bounds hold already at the worst endpoints $A=3\cdot10^{10}-3$,
$t=1/5$.

To use the coefficient bounds of \cite[Proposition 6.2]{P}, take
$K=1$ when $U\ge0$ and $K=\max\{100,\lfloor-U\rfloor+3\}$ otherwise.
For $U\ge0$ the nonconstant coefficient and remainder are bounded by
$0.2\,9^U/(a-0.865)$: from
\eqref{eq:C-positive} and \eqref{eq:RS-positive}, with $K=1$,
\[
 \frac{|C_1|}{a}+|RS_1|
 \le9^U\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,a}
                         +\frac{1.21}{7a^2}\right)
 <9^U\left(\frac{0.2}{a}+\frac{0.173}{a^2}\right)
 \le\frac{0.2\,9^U}{a-0.865}.
\]
At $U=0$ the coefficient bound \eqref{eq:C-negative} suffices as
well. For $U<0$, our choice of $K$ gives $K+U\ge2$, so
\eqref{eq:RS-negative} applies on the entire negative tail.
The first hundred coefficients have
sum at most $0.029\,2^{-U}/a$: define
\[
 P_0=\frac{\sqrt2}{4\pi^2}<0.036,\qquad
 \kappa_0=((3-2\log2)\pi)^{-1/2}<0.445.
\]
Separating the even and odd indices gives
\[
 a\sum_{k=1}^{100}P_0\Gamma(k/2)(\kappa_0/a)^k
 \le P_0\frac{\sqrt\pi\kappa_0+\kappa_0^2/a}
                   {1-50\kappa_0^2/a^2}<0.029.
\]
When $K=100$, the additional $RS_{100}$, including the exponent-error
weight, has Gaussian expectation below $10^{-200}$. Indeed its
coefficient is at most $\tfrac12\Gamma(101/2)(1.1/a)^{101}$,
and $\mathbb E e^{(U^2+1)/A}<2$; use
$\Gamma(101/2)\le101^{101}$ and $a\ge60000$.
For all remaining indices, including the separate remainder index
$k=K+1$, one has $k\le-U+4$. Tonelli's theorem and a Gaussian tail
bound majorize their expectation by
\[
 8\sqrt{t/\pi}\,e^{33/A}
 \sum_{k\ge100}\frac{1.1^k\Gamma(k/2)}{(k-8)a^k}
 \exp\left(-\frac{(k-7)^2}{2t}+(k-7)\log2\right).
\]
Indeed, $U-\sigma\le7-k$, and $U^2+1\le2(U-\sigma)^2+33$.
Use $\Gamma(k/2)\le k^k$, $\log k\le k/4$ for $k\ge100$,
$\log1.1<0.1$, and $\log2<1$. The last display is less than
$8e^{-5000}<10^{-100}$. This proves \eqref{eq:eps}; the small
constant-mode error is below $\tfrac12\cdot10^{-8}$, so it and the
two tails fit inside the $10^{-8}$ allowance.
For its final inequality use $9^\sigma\le9^4$ and $2^{-\sigma}\le8$.

Normalize \eqref{eq:R} by $B_t$. Put $s_+=(1+y)/2+iT$,
$\sigma_+=(1+y)/2$, $\Delta=\sigma_+-i\pi t/8$, and
$L'=\log(T'/(2\pi))$. Taylor expansion from $iT'$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\{\log M_0(s_+)-\log M_0(iT')\}
 =\frac{\sigma_+L'}2+\frac{t\pi^2}{32}+e_1,
 \qquad |e_1|\le\frac{22}{x-20}.
\]
Here $|\Delta|<4$, the linear error is at most $12/x$, and
the quadratic error is at most $8/(x-6)$. Also
\[
 \left|\alpha(s_+)^2-(L/2+i\pi/4)^2\right|
 \le\frac{8\sqrt{L^2+\pi^2/4}}{x-20}
                         +\frac{64}{(x-20)^2}.
\]
Using $L'\ge L$ and $\sigma_+>0$ therefore gives
\[
 \frac{e^{t\pi^2/64}|M_0(iT')|}{|M_t((1+y)/2+iT)|}
 \le2\mathcal Q^{-(1+y)/4}e^{-tL^2/16}.
\]
In this calculation the three terms involving $t\pi^2$ cancel;
a bound for the remaining error in the exponent is
$(22+2t\sqrt{L^2+\pi^2/4})/(x-20)+16t/(x-20)^2<10^{-6}$.
Both real parts $\sigma=(1\pm y)/2$ lie in $[-3,4]$.
Thus both remainder integrals together contribute less than
$4\mathcal Q^{-1}<10^{-8}$. Combining them with the summand errors
proves \eqref{eq:approx}. Dominated convergence gives the endpoint $t=0$.

Finally, if $4\le y\le6$, the first sum differs from $1$ by at most
$\zeta(5/2)-1<0.345$. The reflected sum has modulus at most
\[
 1.01N^{-y}\sum_{n\le N}n^{(y-1)/2}
 \le1.01N^{(1-y)/2}\le1.01N^{-3/2}<10^{-6}.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:approx} this is less than $0.345002<7/20$,
proving \eqref{eq:disk}.

label: prop:density
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:density}
For $x\ge X$ and $0\le t\le1/5$,
\[
 S(x,4,t)>\frac{21}{4}.
\]
head: environment

label: eq:frozen-error
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $z_0=x+4i$ and $t$, and set
$N_0=\lfloor\sqrt{x/(4\pi)+t/16}\rfloor$. On the closed unit disk
$|z-z_0|\le1$ put
\[
 F=H_t/B_t,\qquad P=P_{N_0}(s_B,t),\qquad
 R=\gamma P_{N_0}(s_A,t),\qquad E=F-P-R.
\]
All four functions are holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the disk.
Its points satisfy $\operatorname{Re} z\ge X-1>6\cdot10^{10}$ and
$3\le\operatorname{Im} z\le5$. The pointwise cutoff $N(z)$ in
Lemma~\ref{lem:approx} differs from $N_0$ by at most one, since
$\sqrt{\operatorname{Re} z/(4\pi)+t/16}$ varies by less than one on the disk.
The possible extra index satisfies $n\ge60000$ and $n\le N(z)+1$.
The normalizer bounds in that lemma give a reflected-to-first ratio
below $1.02$ also at $n=N(z)+1$; use
$n\le\sqrt{\mathcal Q+1/80}+1$ and $3\le y\le5$.
Both heat weights still combine as before because $\log n\le L$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frozen-error}
 |E(z)|<10^{-6}+\frac{3}{60000^2}<2\cdot10^{-6},
 \qquad |E'(z_0)|<2\cdot10^{-6}.
\end{equation}
The second inequality is Cauchy's estimate on the fixed-cutoff
remainder. At the centre, $N_0=N(z_0)$ and $|E(z_0)|<10^{-6}$.

Hereafter all quantities are evaluated at $z_0$. The elementary bounds
proved in Section~\ref{sec:checks} are
\[
 Z:=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-5/2}<\frac{269}{200},\qquad
 J:=\sum_{n\ge2}(\log n)n^{-5/2}<\frac{39}{100}.
\]
Since $\operatorname{Re} w=5/2$ and
$|s_B'|\le1/2+t/[4(x-6)]<1/2+10^{-10}$, the heat-weight estimate gives
\[
 |P-1|\le Z-1,\qquad |P'|\le(1/2+10^{-10})J.
\]
For the reflected term, the same estimates give
\[
 |R|\le1.01N_0^{-4}\sum_{n\le N_0}n^{3/2}
       \le1.01N_0^{-3/2}<10^{-6}.
\]
Write $\beta=\alpha+(t/2)\alpha\alpha'$. Then
$\gamma'/\gamma=(i/2)(\beta(v)+\beta(w))$ and
$|s_A'|\le1/2+t/[4(x-6)]$. Thus
\[
 |\gamma'/\gamma|+|s_A'|\log n\le L+2
       \qquad(1\le n\le N_0),
\]
using $|\alpha(s)|\le L/2+1$ and the preceding derivative bounds.
It follows, term by term, that
\[
 |R'|\le1.01(L+2)N_0^{-3/2}<2\cdot10^{-6}.
\]
To check uniformity in $x$, use $\mathcal Q<(N_0+1)^2$ and hence
$L+2<2\log N_0+3$. The function
$(2\log N+3)N^{-3/2}$ decreases for $N\ge60000$; with
$\log60000<12$ and $\sqrt{60000}>240$, its contribution is at most
$1.01\cdot27/(60000\cdot240)<2\cdot10^{-6}$.

Combining these inequalities yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F-logder}
 \left|\frac{F'}F\right|
 <\frac{(1/2+10^{-10})(39/100)+4\cdot10^{-6}}
          {2-269/200-2\cdot10^{-6}}
 <0.297717.
\end{equation}
Finally
\[
 -\operatorname{Im}\frac{B_t'}{B_t}
 =\frac12\operatorname{Re}\left(\alpha(w)+\frac t2\alpha(w)\alpha'(w)\right)
 \ge\frac14\log\frac{x}{4\pi}-10^{-6}.
\]
Section~\ref{sec:checks} gives $L/4>111/20$. Therefore
\[
 S(x,4,t)>\frac{111}{20}-10^{-6}
 -\frac{(1/2+10^{-10})(39/100)+4\cdot10^{-6}}
          {2-269/200-2\cdot10^{-6}}
 >\frac{21}{4}.
\]
This estimate includes the heat dependence for the full interval
$0\le t\le1/5$; it is not a calculation restricted to $t=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The functional equation converts the assumed half-plane to
$M(0)\le a=9/16$. At a simple highest zero $x+ih$, with $q=h^2$,
the paired-zero identity gives
\[
 q'\le-2-\frac{4q}{p}S(x,p,t)+\frac{8q}{p^2-q}
 \qquad(p^2\ge5q).
\]
For completeness, the kernel comparison behind this identity follows
by clearing positive denominators: with $D=d^2$, $A=h^2$, $B=p^2$,
$r=v^2\le A$, its numerator is a positive factor times
\[
 (B-A)\{D^2+(A+B-6r)D+(A-r)(B-r)\}\ge0.
\]
While the comparison height satisfies $q>b$, Lemma~\ref{lem:head}
places a contact zero outside the finite region, so symmetry permits
$x>X$. Proposition~\ref{prop:density}, with $p=4$, then gives
\[
 q'\le-2-\frac{21}{4}q+\frac{8q}{16-q}\le-2-kq,
 \qquad k=\frac{21}{4}-\frac8{16-a}=\frac{4675}{988}.
\]
Here the classical strip theorem ensures $q\le a$ throughout.
Use the barrier
\[
 Q(t)=(a+2/k)e^{-kt}-2/k.
\]
For $0<\varepsilon<1$ let $Q_\varepsilon'=-2-kQ_\varepsilon+\varepsilon$ and
$Q_\varepsilon(0)=a+\varepsilon$. Initially $Q_\varepsilon>a\ge M$, so contact is impossible
on some interval $[0,t_0]$. At a first simple contact while $Q_\varepsilon>b$,
every zero has height at most $\sqrt{Q_\varepsilon}$ and the classical strip
bound still gives $q\le a$. The kernel comparison therefore applies
and gives $q'\le-2-kq<Q_\varepsilon'$, contradicting contact from below.
For a multiple contact, the vertical splitting described in
Lemma~\ref{lem:head} supplies an earlier zero higher by $c\sqrt v$,
$c>0$, whereas $\sqrt{Q_\varepsilon(t-v)}=\sqrt{Q_\varepsilon(t)}+O(v)$.
This also contradicts first contact. Polymath's Theorem 1.5(i) puts
every nonreal zero at $|x|<\exp(C/t)$ for an absolute $C$, uniformly
on $t\in[t_0,1/5]$. Thus contact is attained in a compact set.
Continuous dependence of $Q_\varepsilon$ on $\varepsilon$ allows passage to
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$ up to the time $Q=b$.

The time at which $Q=b$ is
\[
 t_* =\frac1k\log\frac{2+ka}{2+kb}
      =\frac{988}{4675}\log\frac{73691}{34608}<\frac4{25}<\frac15.
\]
Comparison up to this time and continuity give $M(t_*)\le1/25$.
De Bruijn's strip theorem yields $\Lambda\le t_*+1/50<9/50$.
head: environment

label: rem:halfplane
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:halfplane}
Assume more generally that the nontrivial zeros of $\zeta$ have
$\operatorname{Re} s\le\sigma$, with $1/2\le\sigma\le1$. Set
\[
 a=(2\sigma-1)^2,\qquad b=1/25,\qquad
 k_4(a)=\frac{21}{4}-\frac8{16-a}.
\]
If $a\le b$, the classical strip theorem gives $\Lambda\le a/2$.
For $a>b$, define
\[
 T_4(a)=\frac1{k_4(a)}\log\frac{2+k_4(a)a}{2+k_4(a)b},
 \qquad F_4(\sigma)=\frac1{50}+T_4(a).
\]
The preceding proof gives $\Lambda\le F_4(\sigma)$ whenever
$T_4(a)\le1/5$. This time restriction is essential. Also
$4^2\ge5a$ throughout $0\le a\le1$, so the kernel condition
causes no further restriction.

The function $T_4$ increases strictly with $a>b$: its numerator
interval expands while $k_4(a)$ decreases, as is also clear from
$T_4(a)=\int_b^a(2+k_4(a)q)^{-1}\,dq$.
The unique thresholds satisfy
\[
 \begin{array}{lll}
 F_4(\sigma)=1/5:&0.90664<\sigma<0.90665,
       &\sigma\simeq0.9066425127,\\
 T_4((2\sigma-1)^2)=1/5:&0.93835<\sigma<0.93836,
       &\sigma\simeq0.9383580289.
 \end{array}
\]
Thus this formula improves the published $0.2$ below the first
threshold and remains justified up to the second. Beyond the
admissible range use the unconditional bound, not an extrapolation
of $F_4$. Where both apply one may take
$\Lambda\le\min\{1/5,F_4(\sigma)\}$.
head: environment
name: The half-plane parameter and its admissible range

label: lem:heat-gain
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:heat-gain}
For $x\ge X$, $0\le t\le1/5$, $y\ge3$, and $1\le n\le N$,
\[
 |h_nn^{-s_B}|\le n^{-(1+y)/2}
    \exp\left(-\frac t4\log n\,(L-\log n)\right)
 \le n^{-(1+y)/2-2.78t},
 \qquad |n^{-s_B}|\le n^{-(1+y)/2-5.57t}.
\]
head: environment
name: Heat-weight gain

title: Proof
body_md:
Use $\operatorname{Re} s_B\ge(1+y)/2+tL/4$ from the normalizer bounds.
Also $N^2\le\mathcal Q+1/80$, so
$2\log n\le L+3\cdot10^{-12}$ and
$(L-\log n)/4\ge L/8-10^{-12}>2.78$.
head: environment

label: prop:triangle-step
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Triangle estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:heat-gain} gives $|P-1|\le Z(u)-1$ and
$|P'|\le\nu J(u)$. The denominator is positive because
$Z(u)\le Z(\sigma_p)<1.641$, as certified below. Thus
$|F'/F|\le(\nu J(u)+\epsilon_1)/(2-Z(u)-\epsilon_0)$.
Combine this with the normalizer bound.
head: environment

label: prop:euler-step
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Euler-product perturbation estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $s=s_B(z_0)$, with $\operatorname{Re} s\ge\sigma_p+5.57t\ge u$, and
keep $N_0,t$ fixed when differentiating in $z$. Then
\begin{align*}
 P&=\zeta(s)-\sum_{n>N_0}n^{-s}+D_0,
 &D_0&=\sum_{n\le N_0}(h_n-1)n^{-s},\\
 P'&=-s_B'\left(-\zeta'(s)-\sum_{n>N_0}(\log n)n^{-s}+D_1\right),
 &D_1&=\sum_{n\le N_0}(h_n-1)(\log n)n^{-s}.
\end{align*}
The integral test, $\operatorname{Re} s\ge\sigma_p>2$, and $N_0\ge60000$ give
\[
 \sum_{n>N_0}n^{-\operatorname{Re} s}<1.7\cdot10^{-5},\qquad
 \sum_{n>N_0}(\log n)n^{-\operatorname{Re} s}<2.1\cdot10^{-4}.
\]
In $D_j$, the terms with $n\le K_0$ are bounded by the finite sums
in \eqref{eq:delta0}--\eqref{eq:delta1}. For $K_0<n\le N_0$,
\[
 |(h_n-1)n^{-s}|\le|h_nn^{-s}|\le n^{-\sigma_p}.
\]
The corresponding tails above $K_0$ are below $1.6\cdot10^{-5}$
and $1.9\cdot10^{-4}$, respectively. The allowances in the
proposition therefore cover both the zeta tails and the perturbation
tails, whether $N_0\le K_0$ or $N_0>K_0$.

The absolutely convergent Euler product in $\operatorname{Re} s>1$ gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}\right|\le\psi(u),\qquad
 |1/\zeta(s)|\le Z(u),\qquad \rho:=|\zeta(s)|\ge m.
\]
Hence
\[
 \left|\frac{F'}F\right|
 \le\frac{\nu(\psi(u)\rho+\delta_1)+\epsilon_1}
                 {\rho-\delta_0-\epsilon_0}.
\]
This quotient decreases in $\rho>\delta_0+\epsilon_0$, so replacing
$\rho$ by $m$ gives \eqref{eq:euler-step}. The Euler product is used
only for $\zeta$; the heat weights themselves are not multiplicative.
head: environment

label: thm:step
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:step}
Suppose $M(0)\le q_0$ and
$0=t_0<\cdots<t_n\le1/5$. Write $d_i=t_{i+1}-t_i$.
Let $q_0>q_1>\cdots>q_n\ge b=1/25$ and fix $p>0$.
Suppose, for $0\le i<n$, that
\[
 S(x,p,t)\ge C_i\quad(x\ge X,\ t_i\le t\le t_{i+1}),\qquad
 p^2\ge5q_i,\qquad
 k_i=\frac{4C_i}{p}-\frac8{p^2-q_i}>0,
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:step-gate}
 e^{k_id_i}(2+k_iq_{i+1})\ge2+k_iq_i.
\end{equation}
Then $M(t_n)\le q_n$ and $\Lambda\le t_n+q_n/2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Induct on $i$. Given $M(t_i)\le q_i$, the classical strip theorem
ensures $M(t)\le q_i$ for $t\ge t_i$. At a highest simple zero
with squared height $q>b$, Lemma~\ref{lem:head} places the zero at
$|x|>X$, and the paired-zero comparison used above gives
\[
 q'\le-2-\frac{4C_i}{p}q+\frac{8q}{p^2-q}
       \le-2-k_iq.
\]
Compare with $Q_i(t)=(q_i+2/k_i)e^{-k_i(t-t_i)}-2/k_i$ while
$Q_i>b$. The strict perturbed barriers, compact attainment at positive
time, and backward Hermite splitting used in the proof of
\eqref{eq:old-bound} justify this comparison also at multiple zeros.
At the initial time of a step, a small upward perturbation supplies
strict separation; the strip theorem bounds contact heights by $q_i$.
If $Q_i$ reaches $b$ before $t_{i+1}$, then $M\le b$ there and
remains at most $b$ by the strip theorem. Otherwise
\eqref{eq:step-gate} is exactly $Q_i(t_{i+1})\le q_{i+1}$.
This proves the induction. Apply the strip theorem once more at $t_n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The half-plane assumption and the functional equation give
$M(0)\le9/16$. Every row of Table~\ref{tab:eul-steps} satisfies the
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:step}, by the certificates below.
The final time is $t_{15}=7/50+51/12500=1801/12500$, and
$q_{15}=1/25$. Therefore
\[
 \Lambda\le\frac{1801}{12500}+\frac1{50}
          =\frac{2051}{12500}=0.16408.
\]
The same reasoning applied to Table~\ref{tab:tri-steps} gives
$\Lambda\le3793/25000+1/50=4293/25000=0.17172$.
head: environment
name: Derivation of the two intermediate stepped bounds

label: lem:kernel-derivative
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $D=d^2$, $r=v^2$. Direct differentiation gives
\[
 K_p=\frac{2pw}{\Delta},\qquad
 \partial_pK_p=\frac{(2w+4B)\Delta-8Bw^2}{\Delta^2}.
\]
Thus the bracket in \eqref{eq:kernel-derivative} is
$\mathcal N/\Delta^2$. Both $w$ and $\Delta$ are positive.
With $A=h^2$ and $v_0=D+A-r$, we have $v_0\ge D$, $v_0>0$, and
\[
 \frac{K_h}{h}=\frac{2v_0}{v_0^2+4Dr}
 \ge\frac2{v_0+4r}=\frac2{D+A+3r}
 \ge\frac2{D+A_2+3r}.
\]
If $\mathcal N\le0$, the result follows immediately. Otherwise,
$\Phi\ge0$ gives $2/(D+A_2+3r)\ge\mathcal N/\Delta^2$.
head: environment

label: prop:two-density
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All primes below denote complex differentiation in $z$, with $t$ fixed.
Write $H_t=B_tF$. Since $S=-\operatorname{Im}(H_t'/H_t)$,
$\partial_yS=-\operatorname{Re}(H_t'/H_t)'$.

\emph{Normalizer.} Direct differentiation gives
\[
 \alpha''(s)=s^{-3}+2(s-1)^{-3}-\tfrac12s^{-2},\qquad
 |\alpha''|\le2/x^2+24/x^3<3/x^2.
\]
With $\beta=\alpha+(t/2)\alpha\alpha'$, one has
$B_t'/B_t=-i\beta(w)/2$ and $(B_t'/B_t)'=-\beta'(w)/4$.
The bounds already proved for $\alpha$ and $\alpha'$ yield
\[
 |\beta'|\le|\alpha'|+\tfrac t2(|\alpha'|^2+|\alpha||\alpha''|)
 <10^{-10},\qquad |s_B''|\le t|\alpha''|/8<10^{-20}.
\]
More precisely, $|s_B'|\le1/2+t/[4(x-6)]<1/2+10^{-12}$.
Consequently $|s_B'|\le c_1$ and $|s_B'|^2\le c_2$; the latter
inequality is obtained from this sharper bound, not by squaring $c_1$.

\emph{Fixed cutoff.} At $z_0=x+ip$ put $N_0=N(z_0)$ and, on
$|z-z_0|\le r_0$, define
\[
 P=P_{N_0}(s_B,t),\quad R=\gamma P_{N_0}(s_A,t),\quad E=F-P-R,
 \qquad T=F-\zeta(s_B),\quad \varepsilon=T/\zeta(s_B).
\]
The disk lies in $3\le\operatorname{Im} z\le3.1$ and $\operatorname{Re} z>6\cdot10^{10}$.
The cutoff changes by at most one. The same argument as in
\eqref{eq:frozen-error}, with extra summands bounded by
$3/60000^2$, gives $|E|<2\cdot10^{-6}$ on the disk and
$|E(z_0)|<10^{-6}$. Cauchy's estimates therefore give
$|E'(z_0)|\le\eta_1$ and $|E''(z_0)|\le\eta_2$.

At the centre, $\operatorname{Re} s_B\ge u$. The finite perturbation
$P-\zeta(s_B)$ has terms $(h_n-1)n^{-s_B}$ for $n\le N_0$
and $-n^{-s_B}$ for $n>N_0$.
Because $N_0\ge N_*>N_1$, the perturbation tail $N_1<n\le N_0$
and the zeta tail $n>N_0$ are disjoint. Each is bounded by
$n^{-u_8}$, so their union is covered by the single integral tail
in \eqref{eq:new-delta}; there is no omitted zeta tail.
Termwise differentiation then gives
\begin{align*}
 |P-\zeta(s_B)|&\le\delta_0,\\
 |(P-\zeta(s_B))'|&\le c_1\delta_1,\\
 |(P-\zeta(s_B))''|&\le c_2\delta_2+10^{-20}\delta_1.
\end{align*}
Here the integral test applies since $(\log y)^j y^{-u_8}$ decreases
for $y\ge N_1$, $j\le2$.

For $R$, equation~\eqref{eq:reflected-heat} and $e>0$ give
\[
 \sum_{n\le N_0}|\gamma h_nn^{-s_A}|
 \le1.01N_0^{-p}\left(\frac{N_0^{e+1}}{e+1}+N_0^e\right).
\]
A reflected summand $\tau_n$ has $\tau_n'=\lambda_n\tau_n$,
$\tau_n''=(\lambda_n^2+\lambda_n')\tau_n$, where
$\lambda_n=\gamma'/\gamma-s_A'\log n$.
The normalizer bounds give $|\lambda_n|\le L+2$ and
$|\lambda_n'|<10^{-9}$: use
$\gamma'/\gamma=(i/2)(\beta(v)+\beta(w))$ and the bounds for
$\beta'$ and $s_A''$.
Since $L+2<2\log N_0+3$, the preceding sum multiplied by
$(2\log N_0+3)^j$, $j\le2$, decreases with $N_0\ge N_*$.
Indeed, each power of $N_0$ has exponent at most $1-u_8\le-1.025$,
whereas its logarithmic factor contributes at most
$4/(2\log N_0+3)<0.16$ to its logarithmic derivative.
Thus $|R^{(j)}|\le\rho_j$, for $j=0,1,2$.
It follows that $|T|\le e_0$, $|T'|\le e_1$, and
\[
 |T''|\le c_2\delta_2+\rho_2+\eta_2+10^{-20}\delta_1.
\]

\emph{Division by zeta.} Put $\varrho=\zeta'/\zeta$ and
$\iota=1/\zeta(s_B)$. The absolutely convergent Euler product gives
$|\varrho(s_B)|\le\psi$, $|\varrho'(s_B)|\le\psi_2$, and
$|\iota|\le Z$. Differentiation yields
\[
 |\iota'|\le Zc_1\psi,\qquad
 |\iota''|\le Z\{10^{-20}\psi+c_2(\psi_2+\psi^2)\}.
\]
The small $s_B''$ term in this second inequality must be retained.
In the estimate for $(T\iota)''$, the two such contributions total
at most $10^{-20}Z(\delta_1+\psi e_0)$.
Since $Ze_0<1/2$, we have $\delta_0<1/2$ and $e_0<1/2$.
Moreover $\psi\le J(2)<1$ and $\delta_1<7$: the finite part is
at most $(\log N_1)\delta_0<6$ and its integral tail is below
$10^{-3}$. These elementary inequalities are included in
Section~\ref{sec:kernel-checks}. Therefore the contribution is
less than $8\cdot10^{-20}Z$, covered by the allowance $10^{-9}Z$
in $e_2$. Leibniz's rule now proves
$|\varepsilon^{(j)}|\le\varepsilon_j$, $j=0,1,2$.

Finally $F=\zeta(s_B)(1+\varepsilon)$, so
\begin{align*}
 F'/F&=s_B'\varrho(s_B)+\varepsilon'/(1+\varepsilon),\\
 (F'/F)'&=s_B''\varrho(s_B)+(s_B')^2\varrho'(s_B)
       +\varepsilon''/(1+\varepsilon)
       -(\varepsilon'/(1+\varepsilon))^2.
\end{align*}
Combine these identities with
$-\operatorname{Im}(B_t'/B_t)\ge L/4-10^{-6}$ and
$|(B_t'/B_t)'|<10^{-10}$ to obtain \eqref{eq:new-C}--\eqref{eq:new-G}.
In particular, the last $2\cdot10^{-10}$ covers both the normalizer
and $s_B''\varrho$ terms. The time endpoints in the proposition
were inserted termwise in the heat bounds and the positive finite
sums; no monotonicity of $H_t'/H_t$ itself is asserted.
head: environment

label: thm:derivative-step
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:derivative-step}
Assume $M(0)\le q_0<B=p^2$ and choose
$0=t_0<\cdots<t_n\le1/5$, $d_i=t_{i+1}-t_i$, and
$q_0>q_1>\cdots>q_n\ge b=1/25$.
For $0\le i<n$, suppose $C_i,G_i,\lambda_i,\mu_i\ge0$ satisfy
\[
 S(x,p,t)\ge C_i,\qquad \partial_pS(x,p,t)\le G_i
 \quad(x\ge X,\ t_i\le t\le t_{i+1}),
\]
and the polynomial \eqref{eq:kernel-poly}, with
$(A_2,\lambda,\mu)=(q_i,\lambda_i,\mu_i)$, is nonnegative for
$D\ge0$, $0\le r\le q_i$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:new-k}
 k_i=4\left\{\frac{\lambda_i C_i}{p}-\mu_iG_i
       -\frac{2\lambda_i}{B-q_i}
       -\frac{2\mu_i(B+q_i)}{(B-q_i)^2}\right\}>0.
\end{equation}
If $e^{k_id_i}(2+k_iq_{i+1})\ge2+k_iq_i$ for every $i$, then
$M(t_n)\le q_n$ and $\Lambda\le t_n+q_n/2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At a highest simple zero $x+ih$, with $b<q=h^2\le q_i$, symmetry
and Lemma~\ref{lem:head} permit $x>X$. Its velocity is
$h'=-1/h-2\sum'K_h(d_j,v_j)$, where the sum omits its own
conjugate pair and real zeros have half-pair weight.
Every $v_j\le h$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-derivative} applies.
The full sums at height $p$ are $S$ and $\partial_pS$. They converge
absolutely and locally uniformly in $p$ above the zero strip, as do
the differentiated sums: paired summands are $O(d_j^{-2})$ there.
The removed pair contributes
\[
 K_p(0,h)=\frac{2p}{B-q},\qquad
 \partial_pK_p(0,h)=-\frac{2(B+q)}{(B-q)^2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum\nolimits'K_h\ge h\left\{
 \frac{\lambda_i}{p}\left(C_i-\frac{2p}{B-q}\right)
 -\mu_i\left(G_i+\frac{2(B+q)}{(B-q)^2}\right)\right\}
 \ge hk_i/4.
\]
The last bracket decreases with $q<B$. Thus $q'\le-2-k_iq$.
Induction, the strict barriers, compact attainment at positive time,
and backward vertical Hermite splitting are exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:step}; at contact the classical strip theorem gives
$q\le q_i$, which is the polynomial certificate's range. If the
barrier reaches $b$ early, the strip theorem keeps $M\le b$ for
all later times. Otherwise the stated exponential gate gives
$M(t_{i+1})\le q_{i+1}$. The final strip theorem proves the conclusion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The half-plane hypothesis gives $M(0)\le9/16$ by \eqref{eq:M0}.
Use Theorem~\ref{thm:derivative-step} with $p=61/20$ and
Table~\ref{tab:kernel-steps}. Proposition~\ref{prop:two-density},
with $t^-=t_i$ and $t^+=t_{i+1}$, gives the required $C_i,G_i$;
Section~\ref{sec:kernel-checks} supplies all finite certificates.
The final time is $t_{24}=23/200+463/100000=11963/100000$,
and $q_{24}=1/25$. Hence
\[
 \Lambda\le\frac{11963}{100000}+\frac1{50}
          =\frac{13963}{100000}=0.13963.
\]
